title: SERIALIZABLE Key-Range Locks Block Inserts
description: A SERIALIZABLE read takes key-range locks that block inserts into that range; use the weakest correct isolation so writers proceed. Why it matters: choosing the right isolation level is a core production skill -- using stronger guarantees than a query actually needs is a common cause of unexpected blocking.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine reserving not just the tickets that currently exist for a concert, but reserving the entire *range* of ticket numbers from 100 to 200, specifically so that nobody can print a brand-new ticket numbered 150 while you're still counting how many tickets currently exist in that range. That's a stronger, stranger kind of reservation than just "don't touch the tickets that already exist" — it's "don't let anything new show up in this range at all, even things that don't exist yet." This lesson is about exactly that kind of lock, called a key-range lock, and about the very real cost of the strongest standard isolation level, SERIALIZABLE.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** Isolation levels in SQL Server control how strictly the database protects a transaction from being affected by other transactions running concurrently. SERIALIZABLE is the strictest standard level — it guarantees that if you run the same query twice within one transaction, you'll get exactly the same set of rows both times, with nothing added, removed, or changed in between, as if your transaction were the only one running against the database at all. This lesson is about the locking mechanism SQL Server actually uses to deliver that strong guarantee, and about its real side effect on other transactions trying to write.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Ordinary locks, as covered elsewhere in this course, protect rows that already exist — an exclusive lock stops someone else from changing a specific existing row. But SERIALIZABLE promises something stronger than "the rows I already read won't change" — it promises "no new rows will appear that would have matched my query, either," a phenomenon otherwise called a "phantom read." Protecting against phantoms requires locking something more abstract than an existing row, because the thing being protected against — a brand new row that doesn't exist yet — has no row to put a lock on. SQL Server's answer is the key-range lock: a lock on the *gap* between existing index key values, not on any specific row.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** When a SERIALIZABLE transaction runs a range query — say, `WHERE OrderId BETWEEN 100 AND 200` — against a supporting index, SQL Server doesn't just lock the rows that currently exist within that range; it locks the entire range itself, including all the gaps between existing key values, all the way from just before 100 through just after 200. This is what actually delivers the phantom-proof guarantee: since the lock covers the gaps, not just the existing rows, nothing new can be inserted anywhere inside that locked range for as long as the transaction holds it — there's no gap left unlocked for a new row to slip into. That's a powerful, genuinely useful guarantee for certain kinds of correctness-critical logic. But it comes at a real cost: any other session trying to `INSERT` a brand-new row whose key value would fall anywhere inside that locked range has to wait, blocked, until the SERIALIZABLE transaction finishes and releases its key-range lock — even though that other session isn't touching any row the first transaction actually read, only inserting something new nearby.

**Why this matters in production.** Choosing the right isolation level is a core production skill, and SERIALIZABLE's key-range locking is a common, easy-to-miss cause of writers getting mysteriously blocked by a transaction that, from the outside, looks like it's "just reading" — the same surprising "readers can block writers too" theme that shows up elsewhere in this course, but here specifically caused by a *range* query under the *strictest* isolation level, locking gaps rather than existing rows. It's especially easy to reach for SERIALIZABLE by habit, assuming "the strictest option is the safest option," without realizing the concurrency cost that strictness carries — every insert into that locked range, from any other session, simply has to wait its turn.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is choosing the weakest isolation level that's still actually correct for what the transaction needs — if the logic doesn't genuinely require the phantom-read guarantee that SERIALIZABLE provides, a lower isolation level (or a narrower, more targeted locking hint applied only where truly necessary) avoids locking entire key ranges and lets inserts proceed freely, while still protecting whatever the transaction actually needs protected. The broader lesson is that isolation level should be a deliberate choice based on what guarantee the logic genuinely requires, not a default reached for out of an assumption that stronger is always safer with no downside.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs a SERIALIZABLE range query and shows you a concurrent `INSERT` into that same range getting blocked by the resulting key-range lock, even though the insert doesn't touch any row the first transaction actually read. After lowering the isolation level to something that doesn't require phantom protection (or narrowing the locking to what's genuinely needed), re-run the same interleaving and watch the insert proceed immediately, no longer blocked by a lock on a gap it was never actually conflicting with.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** Key-range locking is specific to SERIALIZABLE; the next isolation level down, REPEATABLE READ, protects existing rows from being changed but does *not* protect against phantom inserts, meaning a repeated range query under REPEATABLE READ can return additional new rows on a second read within the same transaction, even though existing rows are guaranteed not to change. Deciding between REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE genuinely comes down to whether phantom protection specifically is required by the business logic, or whether "existing rows won't change" is already sufficient — the stronger guarantee should be a deliberate choice given its real concurrency cost, not a default.

It's worth explicitly checking, whenever SERIALIZABLE shows up in a codebase, whether it was a deliberate choice made for a specific correctness reason, or simply copied from another part of the code without anyone considering the concurrency cost it carries — the latter is far more common in practice than people expect.

## Scenario
A reporting transaction (Session A) counts one customer's orders under **`SERIALIZABLE`** isolation and then does more work before committing. Meanwhile Session B just wants to **insert a new order** for that same customer — and it hangs until A commits, even though B's new row didn't exist when A ran its count.

## Why it blocks
`SERIALIZABLE` guarantees the same query re-run inside the transaction would see **no phantoms** — no rows that appeared after the fact. SQL Server enforces that with **key-range locks**: A's `SELECT ... WHERE CustomerId = 5` locks not just the matching rows but the whole **index range** for `CustomerId = 5` (using `IX_Orders_CustomerId`). B's `INSERT` of a `CustomerId = 5` row must take a range-insert lock in exactly that range, which conflicts — so B blocks for A's entire transaction.

## What to look for
- B waits on a `RangeI-N` / `RangeS` lock (a key-range lock), not an ordinary row lock.
- The block lasts as long as A's `SERIALIZABLE` transaction stays open.

## The concept
Use the weakest isolation that's still correct. Most reporting reads don't need phantom protection; dropping A to the default **`READ COMMITTED`** (or `SNAPSHOT`, which uses row versioning) means A never takes key-range locks, so B's insert into that range proceeds immediately. Reserve `SERIALIZABLE` for the rare case where a repeated read truly must be phantom-free — and keep those transactions short.
startingQuery: -- This is a concurrency lesson. Lower Session A's isolation level so it stops taking key-range locks, then Run the interleaving.
hints: B's INSERT is blocked by a key-range lock, not a row lock. Something made A lock the whole CustomerId = 5 range.
SERIALIZABLE prevents phantoms by locking the index range the query read. That range-lock is what blocks the insert.
Drop Session A to READ COMMITTED (or SNAPSHOT). Then A takes no key-range locks and B can insert into the range: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

interleaving.description: Session A counts CustomerId = 5 orders under SERIALIZABLE (taking key-range locks on that range); Session B's INSERT of a new CustomerId = 5 order blocks behind the range lock.

A.sql: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; BEGIN TRAN; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 5;

interleaving.solutionNote: Lower Session A's isolation from SERIALIZABLE to READ COMMITTED (or SNAPSHOT). Under READ COMMITTED the SELECT takes only brief shared locks (no key-range locks), so B's INSERT into the CustomerId = 5 range is never blocked. Keep SERIALIZABLE only where phantom-free repeated reads are truly required.
